item.title: Venezuela's top economic adviser says aims to publish debt sustainability analysis 'very soon'
item.description: Venezuela is hoping to publish a debt sustainability anaylsis "very soon", but the process has been more challenging than expected, top economic adviser Calixto Ortega told a panel during the IMF-World Bank meetings on on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Rae Wee, Libby George
item.content:encoded: Venezuela is hoping to publish a debt sustainability anaylsis "very soon", but the process has been more challenging than expected, top economic adviser Calixto Ortega told a panel during the IMF-World Bank meetings on on Wednesday. The Latin American oil-producing nation [USN:S0N4040KU TEXT:"announced plans in May to restructure its debt"], and has been working on macroeconomic and debt frameworks to underpin the process since then It had aimed to deliver these in June, and Calixto said they had been "almost ready to do so" before devastating earthquakes struck the country that month "This is a priority," Calixto said of publishing the documents, adding: "I am very optimistic" The restructuring of the country's [USN:L1N43F0Z6 TEXT:"estimated $150-200 billion debt pile"] could be the largest in history and is complicated by a unique web of creditors Calixto also said that dollarisation is "not the right answer" for Venezuela, and that the country needed to strengthen its local currency and strengthen institutions to make economic activity easier He also said Venezuela wants an inflation targeting framework in the medium term, and aims to reach two-digit inflation "sooner rather than later" Venezuela has also been signing agreements this year with gold producers and aims to store gold in the central bank and build up international reserves

item.title: TSX futures rise slightly as yields fall, investors await US CPI
item.description: Futures for Canada's main stock index edged higher on Wednesday as global bond yields continued to ease, while losses in precious metals limited gains ahead of key US inflation data.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Futures for Canada's main stock index edged higher on Wednesday as global bond yields continued to ease, while losses in precious metals limited gains ahead of key US inflation data. December futures on the S&P/TSX index inched up 0.2% at 6:04 a.m. ET (1004 GMT). Oil prices were little changed after gaining earlier in the session following attacks on two vessels in the Strait of Hormuz Reuters reported that Iran was using new tactics to target ships, seeking to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections Silver prices fell over 1% and gold was down 0.4%, while investors braced for [USN:L1N45Z0VZ TEXT:"US consumer price index"](CPI) data due later in the day for clues on the Federal Reserve's monetary policy stance Consumer prices in the US likely surged in September, adding to a string of unfavorable developments for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party heading into crucial November 3 midterm elections Traders are pricing in at least one 25-basis-point rate hike by the Fed before the end of the year, according to LSEG data Yields in the Canadian benchmark 10-year bond eased to 3.869%, while the US counterpart fell to 5.1938% Global AI-related stocks steadied after a steep selloff in the previous session Canada's main stock index rose to a nearly three-week high on Tuesday lifted by energy shares, while a global semiconductor selloff drove investors into government bonds, helping stabilize yields Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi [USN:S0N44S00M TEXT:"is set visit Canada in December"], Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's office said on Tuesday, as both sides seek to conclude a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement at the earliest opportunity FOR CANADIAN MARKETS NEWS, CLICK ON CODES: TSX market report Canadian dollar and bonds report CA/ Reuters global stocks poll for Canada , Canadian markets directory

item.title: Speed of Europe's diesel stock release in focus as IEA meets
item.description: The speed at which Europe plans to release its large diesel stocks will be the market focus when the International Energy Agency meets on Thursday, with analysts saying a rapid draw could push fuel prices lower but have little impact if spread over many months.
item.dc:creator: Robert Harvey, Canan Sevgili, Ahmad Ghaddar
item.content:encoded: The speed at which Europe plans to release its large diesel stocks will be the market focus when the International Energy Agency meets on Thursday, with analysts saying a rapid draw could push fuel prices lower but have little impact if spread over many months. The price of diesel, which powers transport, agriculture and industry, has surged to record highs in many markets as supplies from Russia and the Middle East have fallen, threatening to push inflation and the cost of living higher and adding to pressure on governments. The IEA's governing board will discuss the scale and timing of further stock releases after US President Donald Trump told European Union countries to [USN:L6N45N0J6 TEXT:"draw down emergency inventories"] or face a potential US diesel export ban, as he seeks to lower prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. "The key variable is the pace of the draw," said Abhishek Kumar, analyst at Sparta Commodities. "A 20- to 30-day release would represent a major intervention, while a draw spread over several months would have a relatively smaller impact." A draw of 50 million barrels over 30 days could broadly offset the estimated loss of 1.6 million barrels per day of exports from Russia and the Middle East Gulf, Kumar added. The IEA, which coordinates industrialised nations' releases of oil from emergency stocks during severe supply disruptions, launched a 400-million-barrel withdrawal in March in response to shortages caused by the US-Iran war . Since then, Russian diesel exports [USN:L1N45Y0MF TEXT:"have collapsed"] due to Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries and self-imposed overseas sales restrictions. RELEASES NEED TO BE MAINLY DIESEL, ANALYST SAYS Last week, the IEA said accelerating previously announced releases could rapidly bring another 100 million barrels to market, raising questions over how much genuinely additional supply there could be. "Material impact would only be achieved if the release is imminent and is mainly diesel," said Tamas Varga, an analyst at oil broker PVM. Markets would also want to know whether any release formed part of the original 400 million barrels or came on top of it, he added. Europe holds significant emergency diesel inventories and remains a net importer of the fuel. Reuters reported this month that EU governments were discussing a French proposal for the release of 50 million barrels of diesel, alongside 50 million barrels of crude from IEA members. The [USN:L6N45O0G5 TEXT:"G7 subsequently announced a release"] of 100 million barrels in total. The US said in September it would release the [USN:L1N45L0QS TEXT:"remaining 40 million barrels"] of crude under the March deal, with market analysts suggesting this could be included in Thursday's agreement. IEA chief Fatih Birol on Sunday urged all members to assess whether additional diesel releases [USN:FWN45X02X TEXT:"would be necessary."] Diesel accounts for almost a fifth of the IEA's publicly held emergency stocks. EU IMPORTS OF DIESEL AND GASOIL FALL IN 2026 EU diesel and gasoil imports between March and September fell by 390,000 barrels per day, according to data intelligence firm Kpler. Spread over four months, the release of 50 million barrels of diesel would provide roughly 400,000 bpd according to Reuters calculations, broadly matching the decline in imports. However, any release would need to be balanced with EU rules that require emergency stocks to cover at least 90 days of net imports or 61 days of consumption, whichever is greater. The refining margin for European benchmark diesel futures - or the premium to underlying Brent crude futures - was around $85 per barrel on Wednesday, down from an all-time high of close to $95 per barrel in late September.

item.title: Google DeepMind's Hassabis calls AI hacks 'early warning shots'
item.description: Recent hacking incidents perpetrated by AI agents are "early warning shots", and the world could soon face major incidents if systems are not made more secure, Google DeepMind co-founder and Chair Demis Hassabis said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Padraic Halpin, Yun Chee Foo
item.content:encoded: Recent hacking incidents perpetrated by AI agents are "early warning shots", and the world could soon face major incidents if systems are not made more secure, Google DeepMind co-founder and Chair Demis Hassabis said on Wednesday. Rogue behaviour by AI agents, including corporate network hacks and, most recently, Anthropic's disclosure that an AI model [USN:L6N45V11M TEXT:"submitted a false homicide tip"] to police, has prompted warnings from researchers and fueled concerns over the fast-advancing technology. Hassabis said there was "a lot of work to do" to adopt the kind of best practices that other fields such as biology or the nuclear sector use to secure critical systems and that some sort of international standards body would eventually be needed. "I think these (hacking incidents) are early warning shots for us that systems aren't that powerful yet, so the incidents aren't that major," Hassabis, who is also chief scientist at Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , told an AI summit in Dublin. "But they could be (major) looking into next year and the next couple years if we don't do more work as an industry, as individual companies and governments on securing these systems." He said that, while an international standards body seemed like an obvious intervention, it would need to be nuanced and nimble so as not to stifle innovation. "So what you need to do is basically build up dynamically this kind of certification process that is proportionate with the risks as we see it and can quickly change depending on where the technology goes," he said.

item.title: La pénurie de diesel pourrait se prolonger jusqu'en 2027 - AIE
item.description: Les tensions sur l'approvisionnement en diesel pourraient persister jusqu'en 2027 en raison d'importantes réductions de stocks, contraires à la tendance saisonnière, qui se sont combinées à une production restreinte à l'approche du pic de demande hivernal, déclare l'Agence internationale de l'énergie (AIE) dans son rapport mensuel sur le marché pétrolier.
item.dc:creator: Robert Harvey
item.content:encoded: Les tensions sur l'approvisionnement en diesel pourraient persister jusqu'en 2027 en raison d'importantes réductions de stocks, contraires à la tendance saisonnière, qui se sont combinées à une production restreinte à l'approche du pic de demande hivernal, déclare l'Agence internationale de l'énergie (AIE) dans son rapport mensuel sur le marché pétrolier. Les marges de raffinage du diesel, ou la prime de ce carburant par rapport au pétrole brut sous-jacent , ont atteint des niveaux records de près de 95 dollars (84,81 euros) le baril en septembre. "Les marchés du diesel sont restés soumis à une forte pression, les perturbations prolongées de l’approvisionnement ayant entraîné des prélèvements de stocks contre-saisonniers avant la période de maintenance automnale des raffineries et le pic de demande hivernal", relève l'AIE dans son rapport rendu public mercredi. L’agence prévoit une reprise des activités de raffinage à l’échelle mondiale vers la fin l'année, mais cela ne suffira pas à compenser le déficit accumulé en 2026, précise-t-elle. Les membres de l’AIE coordonnent la mise sur le marché de 100 millions de barils de pétrole et de diesel provenant des réserves stratégiques afin de modérer les prix, dans un contexte de pressions politiques et économiques croissantes. Ce carburant essentiel est largement utilisé dans l’industrie et l’agriculture, ainsi que dans le secteur automobile. Les pertes liées aux exportations de gazole en provenance du Moyen-Orient et de la Russie se sont élevées à 1,3 million de barils par jour au total en septembre, indique l’agence. La demande mondiale totale de pétrole devrait reculer de 2,6 millions de barils par jour en 2026, dont 25% concerneront le gazole. "Les prix record du diesel ont déjà des répercussions économiques généralisées, car ils font grimper le coût des biens et affectent les revenus réels, l’activité économique et l’inflation", explique l'agence. Le 9 octobre, les États-Unis et la Russie ont annoncé un [USN:L8N45V1O6 TEXT:"accord"] pour lever les sanctions sur les exportations de diesel russe, autoriser la livraison de 3 millions de tonnes de ce carburant dans un court laps de temps, selon Donald Trump, et permettre une baisse des prix. Par ailleurs, l’AIE prévoit que l’offre mondiale de pétrole baissera de 5,8 millions de barils par jour cette année, avant de s’inverser pour augmenter de 7,7 millions de barils par jour en 2027, ce qui ramènera le marché mondial du pétrole à un excédent.

item.title: No signs of new EU debt crisis, but prudent fiscal policy is needed - Dombrovskis
item.description: There are no signs of a new euro zone sovereign debt crisis, but governments need to be prudent as debt costs rise on higher sovereign and corporate borrowing and inflation expectations, European Economic Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: There are no signs of a new euro zone sovereign debt crisis, but governments need to be prudent as debt costs rise on higher sovereign and corporate borrowing and inflation expectations, European Economic Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said. Dombrovskis spoke to Reuters at the International Monetary Fund's meetings in Bangkok as the spread of French 10-year bonds over equivalent German paper hovers close to a record 140 basis points, driven by concerns over the country's high debt and deficit and uncertainty about whether a deficit-cutting [USN:L8N44H1DA TEXT:"budget will clear parliament"]. Asked if he saw the makings of a new European sovereign debt crisis after the 2010-2012 turbulence that almost destroyed the euro zone, Dombrovskis said: "No, but obviously we need to be prudent in terms of our fiscal policies." "It is advice which we are giving to EU member states, which is very consistent with the advice the IMF is giving to the broader international community." The 2027 French budget draft envisages a reduction of the deficit to 5.0% of GDP next year from 5.4% expected this year, but campaigning ahead of the April/May elections next year has thrown the passage of the bill in doubt. "France has [USN:L8N45M1N6 TEXT:"presented"] an ambitious budget for 2027, and obviously now it's important that this budget is adopted in due time to provide a signal of clarity and stability about the fiscal outlook in France," Dombrovskis said. He said other EU countries also had debt problems and noted the long average maturity of sovereign debt in Europe now gave governments time to act before the higher yields translated into much higher debt servicing costs.

item.title: Colombia opens embassy in Jerusalem, restores free trade deal with Israel
item.description: Colombia opened its embassy in Jerusalem on Wednesday, becoming the 10th country to do so, as new President Abelardo de la Espriella reversed his predecessor's break with Israel by also restoring a free trade agreement between the two countries.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Colombia opened its embassy in Jerusalem on Wednesday, becoming the 10th country to do so, as new President Abelardo de la Espriella reversed his predecessor's break with Israel by also restoring a free trade agreement between the two countries. Most countries maintain their embassies to Israel in Tel Aviv. Israel regards Jerusalem as its capital, while Palestinians seek East Jerusalem as the capital of a future independent state. The city's status remains one of the most contentious issues in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Former Colombian President Gustavo Petro in May 2024 [USN:S0N3D0083 TEXT:"broke diplomatic relations"] with Israel over its actions in Gaza and had heavily criticised Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu Petro had closed Colombia's embassy in Tel Aviv and recalled its ambassador, a move Israel said was antisemitic and a reward for Hamas militants Right-winger de la Espriella became president in August On Tuesday, the free trade agreement that was terminated by Petro was reinstated Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said: "In just two months, we have reversed most of the negative consequences of the Petro administration for Israel-Colombia relations and have even broken new ground ... I thank ... Abelardo de la Espriella for his determination to bring Israel-Colombia relations to an all-time high" Colombian Minister of Foreign Affairs Omar Bula Escobar attended the opening of the embassy in Jerusalem Several countries have relocated their embassies to Jerusalem since the United States [USN:KBN1I810Z TEXT:"did so in 2018"]. Among them are Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay and [USN:L8N41W1DS TEXT:"Somaliland"]

item.title: AVANT PAPIER Sous pression, les dirigeants de l'UE envisagent d'agir face à la Chine
item.description: Les dirigeants de l'UE se réunissent jeudi à Bruxelles pour examiner l'avenir de leurs relations commerciales avec la Chine, dont les exportations en forte hausse de voitures et d'autres produits manufacturés menace l'industrie locale et risquent de provoquer des licenciements massifs à travers l'Europe.
item.dc:creator: Philip Blenkinsop
item.content:encoded: Les dirigeants de l'UE se réunissent jeudi à Bruxelles pour examiner l'avenir de leurs relations commerciales avec la Chine, dont les exportations en forte hausse de voitures et d'autres produits manufacturés menace l'industrie locale et risquent de provoquer des licenciements massifs à travers l'Europe. Les discussions de ce sommet de deux jours porteront également sur l'Ukraine – notamment [USN:L8N45V1O6 TEXT:"l'accord"] sur le diesel conclu par le président américain Donald Trump avec la Russie –, ainsi que sur le Moyen-Orient, la défense, les migrations, le budget à long terme du bloc des 27 et l'élargissement de celui-ci. Pour certains dirigeants, ce sommet pourrait constituer une répit bienvenu face aux difficultés qu'ils rencontrent dans leur propre pays. Le président français Emmanuel Macron fait ainsi face à des [USN:L8N45Y1K0 TEXT:"manifestations lycéennes"] et à une forte hausse des [USN:L8N45T0QX TEXT:"rendements obligataires"], le chancelier allemand Friedrich Merz peine à remettre sa coalition sur les rails après des [USN:L8N45C09S TEXT:"revers électoraux"] et le président du gouvernement espagnol Pedro Sanchez est à la traîne dans les [USN:L6N45V0J6 TEXT:"sondages"] avant un scrutin législatif anticipé qu'il a lui-même convoqué. En outre, les partis politiques traditionnels sont sous pression partout en Europe face à des formations d'extrême droite et nationalistes portées par le sentiment, chez de nombreux électeurs, que l'économie ne génère pas suffisamment de richesses pour financer le niveau de services publics auquel ils s'attendent. Le double défi que représentent les exportations chinoises à bas prix et la hausse des droits de douane américains exerce une pression supplémentaire sur le tissu industriel des pays de l'UE et entraîne dans certains cas des suppressions d'emplois – comme chez l'Allemand Volkswagen, où 100.000 postes vont disparaître. UN DÉFICIT COMMERCIAL CROISSANT AVEC LA CHINE Dans ce contexte, les dirigeants de l'UE commenceront jeudi par se demander si [USN:L6N45Y0EW TEXT:"l'accord préliminaire"] esquissé avec Pékin afin d'endiguer la vague d'importations de voitures hybrides chinoises constitue une première étape suffisante pour poursuivre les discussions en vue d'un accord commercial plus large, plutôt que d'envisager des restrictions plus sévères. [USN:L6N45R0VW TEXT:"Des propositions franco-allemandes"] ont déjà été présentées concernant d'éventuelles mesures visant à réduire le déficit commercial avec la Chine, qui a atteint 360 milliards d'euros l'année dernière et s'élevait déjà à 200 milliards à l'issue du premier semestre 2026. La présidente de la Commission européenne, Ursula von der Leyen, a qualifié un tel déficit d'"insoutenable" et promis que l'UE utiliserait tous les moyens possibles pour le réduire. L'exécutif européen s'est désormais détourné de l'objectif d'améliorer l'accès des entreprises du bloc au marché chinois pour se concentrer sur la réduction des exportations chinoises au sein de l'UE. Des déficits commerciaux existent dans de nombreux secteurs, notamment ceux des machines, du textile, des métaux de base, des produits chimiques et de l'automobile. Le commissaire européen au commerce, Maros Sefcovic, a qualifié l'accord UE-Chine conclu la semaine dernière de "très bon résultat", précisant toutefois qu'il ne s'agissait que d'une première étape dans un processus plus vaste de rééquilibrage des échanges. Les dirigeants de l'UE devraient demander à la Commission de poursuivre son dialogue avec Pékin, tout en déterminant s'il convient de prendre des mesures supplémentaires. Toutefois, un haut fonctionnaire de la Commission a déclaré lundi que le dialogue seul ne suffirait probablement pas à atteindre cet objectif. Le document franco-allemand publié la semaine dernière souligne l'urgence de prendre des mesures concernant les importations de produits chimiques et de PET, le plastique largement utilisé dans les emballages. Il appelle également à agir pour limiter la dépendance des entreprises à des fournisseurs uniques pour les approvisionnements critiques et à pouvoir riposter rapidement contre les pays portant préjudice à l'UE. La Commission devrait proposer une première mesure de ce type en décembre, même si les dirigeants décident cette semaine de poursuivre le dialogue avec la Chine d'ici là. REVIREMENT DE L'ALLEMAGNE Ce document conjoint marque un revirement de l'Allemagne, qui, il y a seulement deux ans, critiquait ouvertement les projets de l'UE visant à imposer des droits de douane sur les véhicules électriques fabriqués en Chine. Aujourd'hui, Berlin s'est ainsi rallié à la position protectionniste de la France. "Il est significatif qu'un changement de cap qui couvait à Berlin depuis plusieurs semaines et plusieurs mois soit désormais officiel", a déclaré Sander Tordoir, économiste en chef au Centre for European Reform, un groupe de réflexion basé à Londres. "Et il est significatif que les deux États membres les plus importants de l'UE soient clairement sur la même longueur d'onde quant à la manière de faire face au deuxième choc chinois." Pour Emmanuel Macron, qui est sans majorité depuis 2024, la politique européenne reste l'un des rares leviers pour exercer une influence politique et tenter de façonner son héritage, à sept mois de son départ de l'Elysée. Pedro Sanchez, qui a plaidé en faveur d'une ligne plus conciliante envers Pékin alors que son pays accueille de nombreux investissements chinois, risque quant à lui de perdre le pouvoir à l'issue des élections du 29 novembre, les sondages indiquant que le centre et l'extrême droite pourraient réunir suffisamment de voix pour former un gouvernement. À l'inverse, le Premier ministre polonais Donald Tusk et la présidente du Conseil italien Giorgia Meloni abordent relativement le sommet en position de force, même si la hausse de l'inflation et des coûts de l'énergie pèse sur l'Italie. En Pologne, l'action du gouvernement est cependant entravée par le président nationaliste, tandis que la lassitude à l'égard des réfugiés et les craintes d'un débordement de la guerre en Ukraine au-delà de la frontière ont poussé davantage d'électeurs vers les partis d'extrême droite.

item.title: Ohio's working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party
item.description: A decade after Republican Donald Trump peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the November 3 US elections.
item.dc:creator: Richard Cowan
item.content:encoded: A decade after Republican Donald Trump peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the November 3 US elections . Now midway through his second term, the president's magic appears to be losing at least some of its luster with blue-collar men and women as rising prices, the Iran war and concerns about his rhetoric prompt some voters to reconsider their support. The state's reputation as a leading swing state began to fade in 2016 when Trump won strong support from working-class voters who felt their economic concerns were being heard, helping turn Ohio into a reliably Republican state. Almost overnight, Ohio became rock-solid Republican. Ohio voted for the eventual winner in 14 straight presidential elections from 1964 until 2020 when Democrat Joe Biden won nationally but Ohio backed Trump. A shift in Ohio toward Democrats could matter in elections that will help determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress during Trump's final two years in office or hand new leverage [USN:L6N45U0XV TEXT:"to Democrats"] over his agenda. The stakes are high in Ohio, where Republicans are defending a US Senate seat and the governor's office. Two House races are rated [USN:L1N45R0LS TEXT:""toss-ups.""] One, in northwestern Ohio, has long been held by a Democrat and the other, in northeastern Ohio, is Republican-held. Trump is not on the ballot this time but has told supporters to act as if he is. It remains to be seen whether that could end up helping or hindering Republicans running in tough races. Republican Senator Jon Husted is in a tight competition with Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, while Democrat Amy Acton is challenging Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for an open governor's seat. Trump campaigned with Husted and Ramaswamy in Youngstown on Monday to try to energize the Republican base. 'GOD KNOWS WE DIDN'T VOTE FOR THIS' Paul Ringold, a 48-year-old steel hauler and pastor of the mostly Black congregation at the Shalom Church of God and Christ in the city of Warren, embodies the uncertainty that Democrats hope could help them make inroads with working-class voters. Ringold voted for Trump for president in 2016, Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024, but said he remains undecided about whom to support for the US Senate, governor and other offices this year. "I'm in the wilderness trying to find a place," he said. Ringold said rising fuel and food prices and Trump's combative style have left him questioning some of the choices made by a president he once strongly supported. "God knows we didn't vote for this," he said of inflation. Like several voters interviewed by Reuters, Ringold also cited Trump's rhetoric. "I wish he would just tone down that rhetoric ... that old New York in-your-face 'I got you sucker'" persona, he said. EARLY TURNOUT FAVORS DEMOCRATS In early voting that began in Ohio last week, Democrats appeared to be more motivated than Republicans. In Trumbull County, home to the city of Warren and many blue-collar jobs, a strong turnout during the first three days brought 1,224 Democrats to the polls, 559 Republicans and 453 with no known political affiliation, according to county data. Paul Sracic, an Ohio-based senior fellow with the right-of-center Hudson Institute, said "working-class voters, if they are moving at all away from Trump, Brown is a safe landing spot for them" because of the former senator's populist record. "Trump has done a good job of basically focusing on social issues with our guys," said Jose Arroyo, a United Steelworkers official who engages in contract negotiations and labor relations for the sprawling labor union. Trump "seemed to latch on sort of to the dissatisfaction of where the working man has gone. Pensions go away. Plants close. Livelihoods they've always known disappear." The problem, he said, is that focusing primarily on hot-button social issues ignores advancing policies that would "improve the lives of working people" and actually turn them into law. The 50,000 manufacturing jobs in 1990 in the Youngstown-Warren area fell to about 20,000 in 2026, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. In recent years, the Mahoning Valley, long a powerhouse of the steel and automotive industries, has attracted a few new manufacturing plants. Arroyo said the Iran war has boosted domestic oil industry exploration, creating more demand for equipment made of steel. But he acknowledged that the war had also brought higher consumer prices. NLRB 'DISMANTLING' When Trump began his second term in January 2025, he promptly [USN:L2N3OO0LL TEXT:"fired"] two Democratic officials at the National Labor Relations Board and left the agency without the quorum required to take actions. That paralysis lasted [USN:L1N3XM0FP TEXT:"for nearly a year."] Ohio AFL-CIO President Tim Burga cited what he called Trump's "dismantling" of the NLRB as having hindered union organizing efforts and made it harder to contest unfair labor practices and secure work contracts with companies. "We were on a path for the first time in my lifetime, under the Biden administration, for having a national industrial policy," Burga said, but the Trump administration rolled much of it back. [USN:L2N3S70NN TEXT:"Biden and Congress enacted programs"] to spur investment in such industries as clean energy and semiconductors. Trump's trade battles with Canada also were unhelpful to labor, he said. OHIO VOTERS REMAIN DIVIDED Bill Callahan, 75, a self-described Democrat from Cortland, said some relatives who once backed Trump "are traveling back" toward Democrats because "they don't like (politicians) taking money out of their pockets." A part-time warehouse worker from Cortland after a career at General Electric, he said he considered voting for Trump in 2016 but was put off by ethical concerns. Others interviewed by Reuters said higher prices were not enough to change their vote. Joe Scarabino, who co-owns a bait-and-tackle business with his wife Kathryn near Cortland, said the couple responded to higher fuel costs by raising delivery charges rather than product prices, thus having an impact on fewer customers and small business owners. "We believe our Christian values are more than gas prices," he said. The couple declined to say who they support. Retired coal-fired power plant worker Chuck Burns, 67, of Wellsville, credited Trump with reducing illegal immigration and boosting the value of his retirement investments. "He's done a good job ... he's got balls," Burns said. Burns praised Trump's immigration restrictions at the southern border and said his retirement savings have increased in value since Biden left office. Asked what issues worry him in this election season, Burns said, "It's just that Democrats – it's unbelievable some of the stuff that they want to do." Asked to explain, Burns raised transgender issues. "Those poor people, they feel that way, that's fine, that's their business," he said. "They (Democrats) don't need to incorporate our young kids into that stuff."

item.title: BlackRock profit jumps as resilient markets boost fees
item.description: BlackRock posted a jump in third-quarter profit on Wednesday, as the world's largest asset manager raked in higher fees from managing client funds.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: BlackRock (BLK.N) posted a jump in third-quarter profit on Wednesday, as the world's largest asset manager raked in higher fees from managing client funds. Shares of the firm rose 3.1% in premarket trading. Its profit rose to $1.66 billion, or $10.57 per share, in the three months ended September 30, compared with $1.32 billion, or $8.43 per share, a year earlier. BlackRock's assets under management - which determine a large chunk of its earnings - rose to $15.49 trillion, from $13.46 trillion a year earlier. The benchmark S&P 500, which is trading close to its all time highs, continued its steady ascent over the quarter and investors continue to demonstrate their willingness to allocate assets to investment firms such as BlackRock. Asset managers have navigated an increasingly volatile market environment this year, as shifting trade policies and the impact from surging oil prices due to the Iran war have kept investors on edge, but US markets have remained resilient, buoyed by an unrelenting rally in AI-focused stocks. Even as markets have remained sturdy, the combination of surging bond yields and the expectation that the Federal Reserve's recent interest rate hike marks the beginning of a tightening cycle has called into question whether the rally can be sustained. Higher yields over a sustained period can put pressure on markets as investors rotate capital into safe-haven assets, locking in better risk-adjusted returns.

item.content:encoded: S&P 500 and Dow futures edged higher on Wednesday as AI-related stocks steadied after a recent selloff, though elevated oil prices kept investors on edge ahead of key inflation data and another round of bank earnings. Following a mixed bag of earnings from [USN:L1N45Z0O3 TEXT:"Wall Street lenders"] a day earlier, Bank of America (BAC.N) , Morgan Stanley (MS.N) , BlackRock (BLK.N) and State Street (STT.N) are set to report before markets open. Bank of America shares fell 1.5% in premarket trading after the company disclosed a $1.21 billion regulatory fine that could weigh on third-quarter results. Morgan Stanley shares edged 0.7% higher. Chip stocks traded mixed after a sharp pullback earlier this week sparked by reports of progress in chip design by China's CXMT (688825.SS) that fueled concerns about growing competition. Shares of Intel (INTC.O) and Micron (MU.O) fell 1.1% and 1.3%, respectively, while Nvidia (NVDA.O) gained 0.2%. All of the "Magnificent Seven" stocks rose, with Alphabet (GOOGL.O) gaining 0.7%, while Meta (META.O) and Amazon.com (AMZN.O) were marginally higher. At 05:41 a.m. ET, Dow E-minis were up 234 points, or 0.45%, and S&P 500 E-minis were up 16.25 points, or 0.21%. Nasdaq 100 E-minis were down 9 points, or 0.03%. Market participants were also awaiting US consumer price index data, hoping for clues on the Federal Reserve's interest-rate outlook. Economists polled by Reuters estimated headline inflation accelerated to an annual 3.6% in September, with core CPI rising 0.2% on a monthly basis. New York Fed President John Williams [USN:L6N45Z14X TEXT:"said the Fed"] may need to raise its policy rate once more this year to slow inflation, but that he sees no need for hikes in 2027. Remarks from Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin and the Fed’s Beige Book report on regional economic conditions are also due late in the day. Ahead of the CPI data, investors priced in a near 22% chance of a quarter-point US rate hike next week, the CME FedWatch Tool showed. Oil prices[USN:L1N46003I TEXT:" edged higher"], with Brent crude holding above the $100-a-barrel mark after two vessels were struck in the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian officials told Reuters they were deploying new tactics to target ships. Among individual movers, Liquidia (LQDA.O) jumped 49.9% after the drugmaker said it [USN:L6N4600JH TEXT:"settled all six pending lawsuits"] with United Therapeutics (UTHR.O) , ensuring uninterrupted access to Yutrepia, a drug used to treat patients with a form of pulmonary hypertension.

item.content:encoded: Die weltweiten Investitionen in neue Rechenzentren werden sich einer Studie zufolge auf absehbare Zeit nicht auszahlen. Bei Projekten mit einem Gesamtvolumen von 3,5 Billionen Dollar drohten bis 2030 Abschreibungen, wie aus einer am Mittwoch veröffentlichten Analyse der Beratungsfirma Gartner hervorging. Dies sei etwa die Hälfte der Ausgaben in diesem Zeitraum. "Unsere Untersuchungen deuten darauf hin, dass die KI-Umsätze im Geschäfts- und Privatkundenbereich nicht ausreichen werden, um Gewinne zu erzielen", sagte Gartner-Experte Will Sommer. Bis 2030 müssten Rechenzentrumsbetreiber kumuliert 8,5 Billionen Dollar an Umsatz erwirtschaften, um ihre Investitionen zu finanzieren und eine zugrunde gelegte Rendite von zwölf Prozent zu erzielen, rechnete Sommer vor. Die KI-Erlöse in diesem Zeitraum dürften die Marke von 3,6 Billionen Dollar jedoch nicht überschreiten. Zudem müsse die aktuelle Generation an Hochleistungsservern in wenigen Jahren durch modernere Rechner ersetzt werden. Am stärksten wären hiervon die sogenannten Neoclouds betroffen, die sich auf den Betrieb von KI-Rechenzentren spezialisiert haben, schrieben die Gartner-Experten weiter. Sie rechneten damit, dass in den kommenden Jahren 80 Prozent dieser Unternehmen ihren Betrieb einstellen müssen oder übernommen werden. Die großen, Hyperscaler genannten Cloud-Anbieter Amazon (AMZN.O) Web Services (AWS), Google und Microsoft (MSFT.O) verfügten dagegen über ausreichende anderweitige Einnahmequellen, um das aktuelle Investitionstempo aufrechtzuerhalten. Die wieder aufgeflammte Furcht vor einem Abflauen des KI-Booms sorgte in den vergangenen Tagen an den Aktienmärkten für einen [USN:L6N45Z0IH TEXT:"Ausverkauf bei Technologiewerten"]. Vergangene Woche hatte der australische Rechenzentrumsbetreiber Firmus seinen [USN:L8N45U2E0 TEXT:"milliardenschweren Börsengang abgesagt"]. Es wäre das zweitgrößte Börsendebüt in der Geschichte des Landes gewesen.

item.title: Mapping the Market: Dow eyes another run at a rally
item.description: The Dow Jones Industrial Average has been climbing in recent sessions. Even so, it's still closer to its four-month lows than to its record high. Its main index peers, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, both hit all-time highs last week. A new slide looks less likely after the recent bounce, but several hurdles stand between the Dow and fresh peaks, technical analysis suggests.
item.dc:creator: Terence Gabriel
item.content:encoded: The Dow Jones Industrial Average has been climbing in recent sessions. Even so, it's still closer to its four-month lows than to its record high. Its main index peers, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, both hit all-time highs last week. A new slide looks less likely after the recent bounce, but several hurdles stand between the Dow and fresh peaks, technical analysis suggests. Click here for a detailed technical analysis chart . Technical analysis uses past price moves on charts to help map out market scenarios. Chart watchers look for support, a price level that acts like a floor because buyers tend to step in there. They also look for resistance, a level that acts like a ceiling because sellers tend to show up there. One tool for finding these levels is called Fibonacci retracements. Markets rarely move in a straight line. When they pull back after a big move, they often give up a fairly predictable share of their gains, such as 23.6%, 38.2% or 50%. Analysts mark these percentages on charts as possible turning points. Lately the Dow has found support near 51,043. That level is the 38.2% retracement of its rally from March to August, according to data supplied by LSEG. The index dipped below it in late September and early October, but those drops were small and didn't last. For now, bulls seem to be treating that area as a floor. The problem is that resistance sits just overhead. The first barrier is now the 100-day moving average near 52,180. A moving average tracks a market's average price over a set period, smoothing out daily swings to show the underlying trend. The next is the September 22 high at 52,319.01, which makes that area even more important. Past highs and lows matter because prices often stall when they reach them again. Above the September 22 high are the 23.6% retracement at 52,458 and the 50-day moving average, which is falling and currently near 52,591. If the Dow can close above that cluster, it would suggest the rebound is picking up strength. That would put the August highs back in view. However, on Tuesday the Dow hit 52,317.32, essentially touching the September 22 high, before retreating to end at 51,670.10. Bulls will look for the blue-chip average to stabilize and make another go at resistance. If the Dow closes back below 51,403, the recovery would look shaky. Support could then come from the October 1 low near 50,547, the early-February high at 50,513 and the rising 200-day moving average near 50,388, a widely watched measure of the long-term trend. Below there, the June 10 low at 49,909, the 50% retracement at 49,900 and a trendline near 49,800 could all come into play. A trendline is a straight line drawn through a series of past highs or lows. This one runs upward from the April 2025 low. A drop to that zone would leave the Dow roughly 8% to 9% below its record highs. What the chart shows: • Dow holding support near 51,403 • A close above the 52,180 to 52,591 resistance zone would put August highs back in focus • A close below 51,403 risks a slide toward the 49,800 to 50,547 area (Mapping the Market is a daily column written by Reuters journalists. The commentary is based on a technical analysis of financial charts, which helps assess the likelihood of future price moves but does not guarantee the outcome. The column does not constitute investment advice or trading recommendations. )

item.title: Wall Street firms tie bonuses, promotions to AI skills, survey finds
item.description: AI skills are starting to count toward pay and promotion on Wall Street, with nearly a quarter of financial firms tying raises, bonuses or promotions to employees’ proficiency with the technology, a survey showed.
item.dc:creator: Nupur Anand
item.content:encoded: AI skills are starting to count toward pay and promotion on Wall Street, with nearly a quarter of financial firms tying raises, bonuses or promotions to employees’ proficiency with the technology, a survey showed. Another 30% require employees to disclose their use of artificial intelligence tools in formal performance reviews, according to the survey by Selby Jennings, a financial-services recruitment firm. The findings point to a broader shift on Wall Street as firms seek tangible returns from their investment in the technology. "Companies are no longer just seeing if their employees are using AI tools but are also monitoring its impact on output and contribution to business results," Dylan Gomez, executive director at Selby Jennings, told Reuters. "While currently there is no established formula on how much compensation is getting tied to AI usage and performance, we expect this to become more defined by next year," Gomez added. The survey found that 42% of respondents had introduced formal criteria to evaluate employees' AI skills, while 30% had created dedicated teams or roles focused on tracking whether their AI investments were delivering results. The firm polled 500 executives across the finance industry.

item.title: United Auto Workers chief re-elected, now faces tough negotiations and US probe
item.description: United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain’s re-election last week was a breeze. His second term leading the 400,000-member labor group might not be as easy.
item.dc:creator: Nora Eckert
item.content:encoded: United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain’s [USN:L6N45V14E TEXT:"re-election last week"] was a breeze. His second term leading the 400,000-member labor group might not be as easy. Fain became a labor-movement celebrity in 2023, when he took over the UAW and won record contracts after staging multi-week strikes against General Motors (GM.N) , Ford Motor (F.N) and Chrysler-parent Stellantis (STLAM.MI) . His next four-year term presents tough challenges. The Detroit Three will be focused on cutting costs in the next round of contract talks, labor experts said. Fain also is the subject of [USN:L6N43E07V TEXT:"a federal investigation centered on allegations of nepotism"], and he has had an increasingly frayed relationship with the federal monitor overseeing UAW activities. On Tuesday, the federal monitor posted official election results, confirming Fain had won. DETROIT AUTOMAKERS IN COST-CUTTING MODE Faced with higher costs from President Donald Trump's tariffs and elevated commodity prices, the Detroit automakers want to cut labor costs to compete with low-cost Chinese automakers grabbing market share in Europe, Latin America and other regions. “Contract negotiations with the Big Three in 2028 will be much tougher,” said John Logan, a labor professor at San Francisco State University. Fain has rejected the idea that Chinese competition will prevent the auto companies from paying for better labor deals than they did in 2023. “We're not going to stand for China driving a race to the bottom in America," he told Reuters in an interview on Friday. “These companies make massive profits," he said of Detroit. FALLOUT WITH THE FEDERAL MONITOR Fain started his union career working as an electrician at plants owned by Chrysler before the merger that created Stellantis. In the latest round of voting, he sailed to victory in every region represented by the UAW. But the months leading up to the election were marked by turmoil. Since summer, tensions have escalated between Fain and Neil Barofsky, a New York attorney the US government appointed to oversee the UAW. The Department of Justice has launched an investigation into allegations that Fain took actions to benefit his fiancée and retaliated against top union officers. Monitoring of the union is scheduled to end in early 2027, six years after it began. But the monitor could extend the oversight period if it decides that union reforms are insufficient. Fain told Reuters he believes the union is on track to have the monitorship end, and he was proud of the reforms his team made. Fain said the tensions began after the union called for a ceasefire in Gaza in December 2023. In a July livestream to members, Fain said Barofsky disagreed with the union’s stance, and the two had a heated discussion about it. Shortly after that dispute, Fain said Barofsky opened an investigation into whether the union president retaliated against a union official. “I’m not a conspiracy theorist, but I’m also not a freaking idiot,” Fain said in the July livestream, describing the timing of the monitor’s investigation following the intense call. A spokesperson for Jenner & Block LLP, the law firm that employs Barofsky, said in a June statement that Barofsky has "acted with the highest levels of professionalism, integrity, and respect in his roles in public service, private practice, and as a DOJ-appointed monitor.” In the interview with Reuters last week, Fain said he wants to move on from the public dispute and that he was confident the federal investigation would clear him of any suspicion of wrongdoing.

item.title: Inside the booming market for US midterm election bets
item.description: Betting on US midterm elections has surged this year on Polymarket and Kalshi, prediction markets that rose to prominence in 2024 when they bucked traditional opinion polls in signaling that President Donald Trump would win the presidency.
item.dc:creator: Hannah Lang, Michelle Price
item.content:encoded: Betting on US midterm elections has surged this year on Polymarket and Kalshi, prediction markets that rose to prominence in 2024 when they bucked traditional opinion polls in signaling that President Donald Trump would win the presidency. The markets allow traders to buy and sell binary "yes" or "no" contracts on an array of race outcomes, such as which party will control Congress and which candidate will win individual races, as well as on questions such as when candidates may drop out. Although election bets remain a small slice of overall trading on prediction markets, some policymakers and public advocacy groups worry they could undermine [USN:L6N41V1AT TEXT:"faith in the integrity of US democracy"] and provide new avenues for insider trading. Kalshi has suspended a handful of candidates for betting on their own races, while public broadcaster NPR reported in May that campaign staffers were also betting on the races they worked on. Polymarket, Kalshi and other platforms say their markets help reveal accurate, unbiased information. They also say they are [USN:L6N44P0U4 TEXT:"well equipped to guard against misconduct"], and routinely refer cases to US authorities. Kalshi blocks election trades by politicians and campaign workers. But most Americans [USN:L1N45S0TL TEXT:"oppose using prediction markets"] to wager on elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll published Monday. "Election prediction markets focus a disruptive new financial technology on our democratic process," said Michelle Kendler-Kretsch, a researcher at the Washington-based Anti-Corruption Data Collective (ACDC), which has researched betting patterns using data publicly disclosed by the platforms. "This data is bottom-up, not elites-driven," said a Kalshi spokesperson. "Prediction markets are a way to see what people are saying when there's money on the line." Polymarket's election markets have a 98% accuracy rate one day before an election, a company spokesperson said. "We’re providing reliable information to a public that is starved for it. We use state-of-the-art surveillance and dedicated detection systems built for political markets." ACDC analyzed more than 21,000 markets on 2026 US congressional midterm elections across Kalshi and Polymarket's international and US platforms, through September 30, comparing them to 463 markets on the 2024 congressional races. This cycle, the number of markets quickly eclipsed 2024 and continued to surge as the election neared. While more congressional seats are covered this cycle, the number of markets for each race has also grown, focusing on more detailed and precise race variables, according to ACDC. Across the three markets, traders have bet more than $220 million so far this cycle, compared with $92 million for the entire 2024 cycle, according to ACDC. In 2024, wagers continued even after Election Day, as the outcome of some races hung in the balance. In 2024, 71% of election markets were on who would win a race. This cycle, only 16% of markets relate to winners, with the majority – 58% – focused on the margin by which a candidate will win. There are also more markets this cycle on voter turnout for a race. However, the vast majority of overall volume is still wagered on who will win, with many of the more esoteric election markets barely traded, according to Kendler-Kretsch. Overall, election bets are highly concentrated. Most of the $220 million in trading volume is on a few races, most notably the Texas Senate race, in which Democratic candidate James Talarico faces Republican Ken Paxton for an open seat. Traders are also betting heavily on the Senate races in Maine, Michigan and South Carolina, ACDC said. Data from Polymarket's international platform, which also provides data on accounts or "wallets," suggests a few traders dominate election bets. The top 1% of wallets on Polymarket, ranked by trading volume on congressional markets, are responsible for 70% of all congressional betting volume this cycle, according to ACDC.

item.title: Nicaraguan families beg for answers as dissenters vanish into state custody
item.description: Thelma Brenes grew worried when her father in Nicaragua did not return her messages.
item.dc:creator: Gabriela Selser, Diego Oré
item.content:encoded: Thelma Brenes grew worried when her father in Nicaragua did not return her messages. Retired Army Colonel Carlos Brenes, 71, lived with his wife, Salvadora Martinez, 69, on a rural property south of the capital Managua. Brenes' daughter Thelma, living in the Netherlands, asked a neighbor to check on the couple. He found the house empty. Local residents later told her they’d seen the police escorting the couple away in a patrol car. That was August 2025. Since then, the Brenes family have pleaded with the authorities for information about the couple’s whereabouts, health and status, but they have heard nothing, not even if they are in custody. What they do know is that Carlos Brenes is one of President Daniel Ortega's most outspoken critics. Martinez is a homemaker with no known political involvement. "For us, as family members, this is a form of torture," said Thelma Brenes. She is one of growing number of Nicaraguans who say their loved ones have been forcibly disappeared by the government of Ortega. The leader rose to prominence in the leftist Sandinista movement in the 1970s, battling to overthrow the Somoza dictatorship that itself arrested and forcibly disappeared suspected dissidents. One of those who fought alongside Ortega was Carlos Brenes. After Somoza's 1979 ousting, Ortega ruled the country, first as provisional government leader and then as president. He returned to office in 2007, and has ruled Nicaragua continuously since then. During this time, the United Nations, international human rights groups and [USN:S0N41D00X TEXT:"regional leaders"] say, he has consolidated an increasingly [USN:L3N3VQ1KY TEXT:"authoritarian system"], especially since anti-government protests in 2018. The Nicaraguan government did not answer detailed questions regarding the Brenes and Martinez case. The Interior Ministry, Attorney General's Office and the Nicaraguan Army did not respond to requests for comment. TOOL 'TO SOW FEAR' Human rights groups like Memoria y Justicia, led by Nicaraguans in exile, and relatives of political prisoners said that at least 68 people were imprisoned in Nicaragua for political reasons as of the end of September, including 31 victims of enforced disappearance. The UN defines enforced disappearance as the deprivation of liberty by agents of the state, followed by concealment of the person’s whereabouts. Family members told Reuters that the Nicaraguan authorities offer no justification for the detentions: they rarely confirm an arrest, schedule court hearings, or provide information to families. People simply vanish. Last month, three [USN:L6N45D0OQ TEXT:"UN experts"] asked to investigate human rights in Nicaragua said they had documented imprisonment, torture and persecution on political grounds as part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians. According to the UN experts, at least eight people detained for political reasons [USN:L6N42803F TEXT:"have died in state custody"] since the [USN:KCN1IT1XU TEXT:"political crackdown"] began in 2018. They said they have verified 161 cases of enforced disappearance since April 2018, ranging from a few days to several years. The Ortega government has dismissed critics as "fascists" and "coup mongers" and has not commented on the accusations of disappearances. The UN said it has received no official response from Managua to requests for comment sent since 2018. "The government uses enforced disappearance as a deliberate strategy: to sow fear not only among the detained person, but also among their family members, and to warn the entire society: ‘This could happen to you,’" said Reed Brody, a member of the UN Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua. The tactic is not new to Latin America. In previous decades, military dictatorships in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and other countries carried out enforced disappearances as part of widespread repression to keep the regimes in power. 'NO ONE HAS SEEN HIM IN MORE THAN TWO YEARS' As a student, Carlos Brenes joined the protests against Anastasio Somoza, the last of a family clan that ruled Nicaragua for four decades. Brenes enlisted in the revolutionary Sandinista National Liberation Front and helped plan the insurrection that overthrew the dictatorship in 1979. But around 1992, he became disillusioned with Ortega and retired from the Army. In 2018, he once again joined mass protests — this time against the Sandinista government. He was jailed on terrorism charges and released after 10 months. Then, in 2025, he disappeared. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights said in an April report that it had been informed unofficially that Brenes and his wife were tried for treason and sentenced to 15 years in prison. The family said they were not informed of the proceedings and feared for Brenes' health because he suffers from diabetic neuropathy. The Court called on the Nicaraguan government to protect the lives of the couple and other political prisoners and provide information about their whereabouts. The Nicaraguan government has not replied. Brenes is not the only ex-Sandinista who has disappeared. Victor Boitano, 65, the son of an Italian father and a Nicaraguan mother, joined the guerrilla movement at the age of 12, inspired by the example of his mother, who was tortured by the Somoza dictatorship for her political activism. During the revolution, he trained at military academies and rose to the rank of colonel in the Army, but retired in 2007 and began to accuse the Sandinista government of corruption and political crimes. In April 2024, armed police and plainclothes officers arrested him without a warrant at his home in Managua, said his wife, Eugenia Valle, who witnessed the event and says she was hit by an officer during her husband's arrest. He disappeared into the prison system. Valle went from one prison to the next trying to find him, but said the guards always directed her elsewhere. The Nicaraguan Presidency, Interior Ministry, Attorney General's Office and the Army did not respond to a series of detailed questions regarding Boitano's case. Six months after his disappearance, Valle fled the country after her housekeeper called her and told her there were some 30 police officers surrounding her house. Now in exile in Italy, she said she barely sleeps three hours a night and is racked by worry over the fate of her husband, who suffers from hypertension and diabetes. "We don't know what's happening, how he is, or where he is," said Valle. "No one has seen him in more than two years."

item.title: Nine ways the Trump administration could interfere with the midterms
item.description: Reuters asked dozens of election administrators and legal experts what they fear could happen before and after Election Day. While many officials expressed confidence in elections in their own states and counties, they pointed to a broad array of risks.
item.dc:creator: Mike Spector, Linda So, Peter Eisler, Ned Parker
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump has made no secret of his desire to exert control over the country’s upcoming midterm elections. He has urged Republicans to “nationalize” voting, pressed for restrictions on mail-in ballots and deployed federal law enforcement to pursue discredited fraud claims. At a Republican Party convention in September, he called on supporters to “cheat like hell” whether they’re “registered or not.” All of that raises a question: If Trump wanted to follow through, could the president disrupt the election? And how? To answer that question, Reuters interviewed more than 50 election officials, voting experts and election lawyers, and reviewed Trump's public statements, court filings and actions by federal agencies. Their assessments point to a range of scenarios, outlined below, in which the administration could test the boundaries of federal authority.
